title: The Skaldic Interface — Editor Intro
summary: Editorial opening splash that re-arms the live pressures entering Issue 7 without recapping the prior issue or revealing later issue payoffs.
settingText: Neighborhood public library entrance and first view of shelves, daytime
panelPlan: Full-page editorial/title splash at the threshold of an ordinary neighborhood library. Gunnar's line of sight should travel from the small entrance into deep shelves and reading tables that seem to contain far more city than the building's exterior promises.
Bjorn and Carrie can flank the threshold, but Gunnar owns the visual question. Keep the library civic, used and human rather than cathedral-like.
Use shelf gaps, high wall space and quiet reading-room negative space for the captions. Let the short words 'Shelved. Indexed. Borrowed. Argued over.' step the eye deeper into the page.
Do not show the historical dispute, catalog solution, library card, borrowing outcome, book-return obligation, or the final shared-reading payoff.

title: What Happened While We Were Here
summary: The morning after the financial issue, Gunnar reads a free newspaper for interest rather than navigation and discovers that he wants context the household cannot supply itself.
panelPlan: Wide: Morning in 5B. The household ledger from the previous issue remains open on the table beside breakfast. Gunnar reads a free local newspaper folded away from the financial pages.
Medium: Bjorn notices Gunnar is reading instead of checking a route or list.
Close: Gunnar scans local events, short notices and city reporting with genuine interest.
Medium: Carrie enters or looks over from the table while Gunnar asks a question that is not tied to any required errand.
Wide: The others keep eating while Gunnar keeps the paper.

dialogueInline.text: Does it say where we're going?
I want to know what happened while we were here.
That's a bigger project than breakfast.

dialogueInline.text: No one told me to be quiet.

title: Too Much Memory
summary: The library's scale registers not as magic but as an enormous accumulation of other people's remembered work.
panelPlan: Wide: Long but ordinary rows of shelves, patrons seated at tables, returns cart, computers and children's area all visible in one lived-in public interior.
Medium: Gunnar slowly turns, taking in the number of shelves rather than any single object.

Two-shot: Gunnar and Bjorn quietly estimate what the room represents.
Medium: Carrie continues toward the copier, letting them make their own sense of it.

dialogueInline.text: All of these were written by people?

dialogueInline.text: I need two copies and one city record. That's my problem.

title: Meant To Be Heard
summary: Gunnar recognizes the oral structure inside written verse and tests the text quietly aloud, making the library's stored words feel closer to a living skaldic tradition.
panelPlan: Medium: Gunnar reads the book silently at a table; Bjorn arrives carrying a different book.
Close: Gunnar quietly mouths a short generic rhythm from the page without reproducing any real copyrighted passage.
Two-shot: Bjorn notices the cadence rather than the content.
Medium: Gunnar taps the rhythm once with a fingertip on the page.
Close: He looks at the printed lines with new appreciation.

dialogueInline.text: I can hear where it turns.
I can. Hearing it is different.
Then part of the writing is sound.
Then it was meant to be heard.

title: Why Keep A Wrong Book
summary: Bjorn asks the question beneath his irritation: why would a library preserve a book known to contain errors? The answer reframes the institution as storage of claims, not an oracle.
panelPlan: Medium: Bjorn places the completed feedback form beside the book.
Two-shot: He asks the librarian directly why the book remains if it can be wrong.
Medium: The librarian answers plainly, without defending the book as authoritative.
Close on Gunnar: He understands the distinction immediately.
Wide: Behind them, shelves hold many mutually different books.

dialogueInline.text: If it is wrong, why keep it?
Enough to exist. Not enough to be right.
Then how does the next reader know?
They compare it with other books. Dates. Sources. Evidence. Later work.
So the shelf does not decide which one wins.
You keep the mistake beside the correction.
Sometimes the correction gets corrected too.
That is less foolish than I thought.

title: The Skaldic Interface
summary: The issue closes with Gunnar turning written material back into shared spoken experience; the library has become useful not because it replaces oral culture, but because it gives the household more voices to bring into the room.

title: Next: Provision
summary: Editorial closing splash that turns the issue's surviving pressure toward what comes next without summarizing the issue or spoiling the next issue's payoff.
settingText: Bushwick street in early spring with budding trees and changing weather
panelPlan: Full-page closing teaser in unmistakable early spring: new green buds, cool air, wet pavement, layered clouds and ordinary city food deliveries moving through the street.
Bjorn and Gunnar should be looking at the season rather than admiring it; Carrie reads the same mild day as ordinary. The tension is entirely in what each side thinks the calendar means.
Integrate captions through sky and building-edge negative space. Make 'winter is coming' visually small and practical, not ominous fantasy language.
Do not show the bus-stop conversation itself, public-land dispute, community-garden idea, storm preparation, storm arrival, or Issue 8 outcome.
